en: In the *Tathāgatabimbakārāpaṇasūtra* (Tbks 2r1), those whose hearts were filled with wonder spoke thus:
"Oh, the greatness of the power of the fruit of merit!"
"Aho! The power of merit! they said, and became silent.
Then Suvarṇaprabha, together with his retinue, circumambulated the Blessed One, bowed his head in prostration, and sat down near the Blessed One for the purpose of hearing the Dharma. Then...

The Blessed One, knowing the underlying doubts of all sentient beings, for the sake of that great multitude of people who were listening to the Dharma, [expounded] a discourse connected with the Four Noble Truths and characterized by dependent origination, consisting of various types of teachings intended to demonstrate the cause for the arising of power through the fruit of the merit of the former good conduct of that Prince Suvarṇaprabha.
He taught the Dharma-discourse,
which is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end; he elucidated the holy life that is meaningful, well-phrased, absolute, complete, pure, and pristine.
Monks, in the past, in a time long gone, ninety-one aeons ago,

there appeared in the world a perfectly awakened Buddha named Vipaśyin— one endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. Having performed his Buddha-deeds and the task of training his disciples, he passed into final Nirvāṇa like a fire whose fuel has been exhausted.

Monks, there was a certain man who, despite being harsh, poor, and engaged in the labor of farming without respite, became inspired with faith in the teaching of the Blessed One Vipaśyin and made an image of the Blessed One Vipaśyin.

At that time, at that very moment, it was this same Prince Suvarṇaprabha who, by the power of the accumulation of the fruit of merit from having had an image of the Blessed One Vipaśyin made, experienced divine pleasures, enjoyments, sovereignty, and greatness. This is that Prince Suvarṇaprabha;
in brief, monks, I shall describe all his births.

Endowed with the seven precious jewels, he possesses the sovereignty of a glorious universal monarch; he is the lord of the four continents, moving through the expanse of the sky, his movement proceeding unhindered by means of the precious wheel.
O Lord of Lords!
A hundred thousand times he was a universal monarch, a king who ruled over the four continents.
By this very ripening of the meritorious fruit of the Buddha-image, in such a manner,
O monks, he became the king Indra of the gods one hundred thousand times in each of the celestial realms belonging to the desire world;
likewise, he became the sovereign Brahmā one hundred thousand times among the ten classes of the Brahma-world.
Monks, in hundreds of thousands of births, both in direct and reverse order, he was born as a king in ten million families of kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, lords, and sovereigns;
such was he, monks.

Endowed with good fortune, beauty, splendor, renown, fame, and strength, he passed away from heaven and was born into a royal family of sovereign power— born of the highest lineage, born of the unsurpassed lineage.

"Prince Suvarṇaprabha shall, in the presence of gods and humans, attain the state that is unfailing, ageless, deathless, auspicious, and peaceful. Therefore, monks, listen to the power of the fruit of merit from the image of the Buddha belonging to this Prince Suvarṇaprabha; for among those born as human beings, monks, one who desires the welfare of oneself and others should indeed have an image of the Buddha made.
It is as follows, monks: it may be made of clay,
or made of stone, or made of ivory.
Whether made of wood, or made of gold, or made of bronze.
or made of copper, or made of silver, or made of crystal;
Or an image of the Buddha made of precious gems, or made of bronze, or one that is yet to be fashioned.
Whether long or short,
or together with its constituent elements.
Or, having had an image of the Buddha made together with [a representation of] dependent origination,
and having installed it, [one should worship it] with scented water, flower-water, and so forth.

O monks, for any son of good family or daughter of good family who, having bathed and honored [the image] with special offerings, there arises a mass of merit, a heap of merit, an immeasurable and uncommon outflow of the fruit of the merit of that Buddha-image.
Furthermore, monks, it is called "a mass of merit comparable to the infinite."
Whosoever it may be— a monk or a nun, a layman or a laywoman, or a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa,
or a vaiśya—
Even a Śūdra, in such births,
becomes one who retains what he has heard and becomes one who remembers his past lives.
He becomes one whose words are accepted by his kinsmen, retinue, female and male slaves, laborers, servants, and so forth.
He possesses a form beloved by all sentient beings;
he possesses all the marks of excellence; and he becomes a sovereign over all sentient beings.
He becomes endowed with the qualities of all Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and Arhats;
he is constantly devoted to the thought of awakening (bodhicitta),
whatever he desires wherever it may be.
In each and every case, one obtains this;
one becomes free from the afflictions and so forth, such as passion, hatred, delusion, envy, stinginess, greed, and thirst.
"Monks, I say that one attains Buddhahood without interval and swiftly attains the peace of final nirvāṇa.
For what reason? Because it is the power arising from an infinite fruit."

“Monks, I declare that the manifestation of the power of the fruit of merit from a Buddha image, and the ripening of the fruit of merit from a Buddha image— even though the Blessed Buddha has attained final nirvāṇa— he is not as if extinguished, for he is realized through the sight of a Buddha image. Thus spoke the Blessed One, and furthermore, he uttered this verse:
In the past, that lord of brahmins fashioned a supreme image of Kāśyapa and bathed it with scented water;

with fragrant flowers and most delightful perfumes, by that very merit he was liberated from existence. He became stainless, freed from the stains of the afflictions, and attained the state of mastery over the mind.
Never satiated by gazing upon his form, they bathe that image of the Jina;
(2) women and men in this world obtain various enjoyments of diverse kinds, with a splendor of brilliance exceeding that of the moon, sun, and Mercury, as they bathe that image of the Jina. (3)

Men or women whose minds are liberated from the darkness of the afflictions and who are like the full moon dispelling the darkness of delusion— whether they be men or women— attain the state of peace by bathing this image of the Jina, even while casting off their bodies right here. 4 (Tbks 4v4) Men or women, having abandoned the physical body in this very world...
They go to heaven, perfectly at ease for many hundreds of kalpas;
they obtain incomparable happiness with the apsarases. The Buddha declared that this is the noble fruit of such an act for the whole world. 5.
Possessing the divine waters of glorious beauty, with the splendor of virtue and form, and endowed with good fortune, luck, excellent happiness, eloquence, and clarity of speech;
he possesses gentle brilliance like the rays of the sun and moon.

A person who has an image of the Buddha made shall obtain as many kingdoms in heaven and on earth as there are atoms in the stupas of the Blessed One or in his images. They will certainly receive that many realms for having performed that deed.
Indeed, for the sake of the relics of the Buddhas, the Blessed One has manifested bodies;
by means of each subtle atom produced from a single heap of marvelous merit,
he has formed the image of him whose fame pervades the three worlds and whose renown is celebrated in all directions, he who possesses the strength of the Ten Powers.

Those mortals who, having had [this image] made, worship it properly with a joyful mind, obtain a form in heaven and on earth that delights the eyes and shines like pure gold; having attained this, those seekers of peace reach this incomparable happiness frequented by the Victors. (8)

Having heard such a teaching of the Dharma, which was appropriately connected to the origin of gold, Prince Suvarṇaprabha— accompanied by a retinue of five hundred thousand women from his inner apartments— abandoned all his domestic life, including the joy, happiness, and prosperity arising from the merit of the Buddha’s likeness, and likewise went forth into homelessness within the Teaching.

Having applied appropriate mental attention (*yoniso manasikāra*), they abandoned all afflictions and attained arhatship; surrounded by female attendants, they were equal-minded toward a clod of earth and gold; they had done what was to be done, laid down their burdens, exhausted the fetters of existence, and were liberated from the bonds of *saṃsāra*;
their pair of feet were venerated by all the gods, and they were perfectly awakened.
This sutra reveals the greatness of the magnificent manifestation arising from the fruit of merit of a Buddha image.
Thus spoke the Blessed One; those monks, with uplifted minds, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. The monks became Arhats counted among the ranks of the four directions.
This sutra, which reveals the fruit of merit of a Buddha image, is completed.
The Sūtra on the Commissioning of an Image of the Tathāgata is completed.
